query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a low‐temperature stress‐relief annealing post treatment to additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi components will reduce residual stresses, reconfigure dislocation structures, and thereby improve ductility and fatigue performance compared to conventionally produced high-thermal-load AM parts.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built miniature components produced from AlCrFeNiSi powder via laser additive manufacturing, characterized by high residual thermal stresses, microstructural anisotropy, and defects related to rapid solidification.
generation.intervention: Post‐processing stress‐relief annealing at approximately 400°C for 2.5 hours followed by free cooling to room temperature.
generation.conditions: Applicable to miniature components fabricated by laser AM; the treatment should be uniformly applied to parts of dimensions permitting even heating, with subsequent testing via tensile, fatigue, and residual stress measurements (e.g., XRD under standard laboratory conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction and rearrangement of dislocation structures and grain boundaries, leading to lower internal stresses and more homogeneous microstructural characteristics.
generation.mechanism: The modest thermal energy delivered at 400°C is sufficient to allow dislocation motion and recovery without triggering recrystallization or significant grain growth. This enables the relaxation of residual stresses generated during the rapid cooling of AM while maintaining microstructural stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions, the annealed parts will show significantly lower residual stress, improved ductility and fatigue performance, with a modest reduction in yield strength that is acceptable for miniature components.
generation.baseline: High-thermal-load AM components without post-treatment, which typically exhibit high residual stresses, degraded ductility and fatigue properties, and increased processing complexity.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in components with sufficient thermal mass and sizes that allow uniform heat treatment; its effectiveness may diminish in larger components or in materials that undergo undesirable phase transitions even at low temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in mechanical properties and the acceptable trade-off in yield strength reduction remain to be determined, as well as potential interactions with AM-induced anisotropy.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature components from AlCrFeNiSi powder via laser AM. Subject one set to the proposed 400°C for 2.5 h annealing treatment, while keeping the other set as-built. Characterize residual stresses (via X-ray diffraction), perform tensile testing to assess yield strength and ductility, and conduct fatigue testing under cyclic loading.
measurements: Tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Fatigue life under standardized cyclic loading conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the stress-relief annealed group does not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stress and measurable improvements in ductility and fatigue performance, relative to the as-built group, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy has wide application prospects as a biomedical material, and the use of laser additive manufacturing can solve the forming problems faced by the alloy. In view of the characteristics of the one-time forming of additive manufacturing methods, it is necessary to develop non-mechanical processing modification methods. In this paper, deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) is first applied to the modification of a HEA with BCC structure, then the post-processing method of DCT is combined with laser melting deposition (LMD) technology to successfully realize the coordinated improvement of forming and strength–ductility synergistic improvement in lightweight Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr alloy. The final tensile strength of the alloy after DCT treatment is 25% higher than that of the as-cast alloy and 11% higher than that of the as-deposited alloy, and the elongation is increased by 48% and 10%, respectively. In addition, DCT also achieves induced phase transition without additional deformation.Keywords: laser melting deposition, high entropy alloy, deep cryogenic treatment, 3D printing, defects, strength–ductility synergistic improvement

Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) exhibit excellent casting properties and comprehensive mechanical performance, making them suitable for fabricating spatial engineering components using additive manufacturing techniques. However, the rapid solidification process also leads to increased internal stress and reduced structural stability in the components. Therefore, this study focuses on the AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA as the research subject, utilizing laser additive manufacturing to fabricate components and systematically investigating the influence of heat treatment processes on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the components. The research demonstrates that low-temperature heat treatment (700 °C and below) acts as a stress relief-annealing process for the components. The yield strength decreased from 1003.2 MPa to 742.1 MPa. At 900 °C heat treatment, the constraining effect between recrystallized grains and surrounding grains outweighs the dislocation release effect caused by recrystallization, resulting in an increase in dislocation density. A batch of tensile specimens was tempered to reduce residual stress [] resulting from the printing process, which is typical of additively manufactured parts []. Heat treatment was conducted at 400 °C for 2.5 h aimed at achieving stress relief and subtle microstructural adjustments without triggering significant phase transformations or coarsening. Studies on similar HEAs show that annealing at low to moderate temperatures (300–500 °C) can reduce internal stresses and dislocation density but may also slightly decrease strength or ductility due to recovery processes, while avoiding the pronounced softening, grain growth, or phase separation that occur at higher temperatures (above 700–800 °C) []. In CoCrFeNiCu systems, higher temperature treatments (e.g., 800–1100 °C) can lead to the precipitation and coarsening of Cu-rich phases, transformation between FCC phases, and a general reduction in hardness and thermal stability due to microstructural coarsening and phase changes []. Furthermore, in situ tensile testing using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) was conducted to characterize the deformation behavior and crack propagation mechanisms at the microscale.

chosen.approach: Post‐treatment heat processing for residual stress relief
